processing: Made either by simmering dried apple pieces, or from instant granules or powder based on concentrated apple juice and sugar.
harvest_season: No harvest season applies: dried fruit and instant mixes are available all year.
appearance_dry: Pale dried apple pieces, or fine sugary granules or powder.
appearance_wet: Soft pale apple pieces, or nothing at all with the instant kind.
taste_profile: Sweet, mild apple, tart at the edge when made from real fruit and closer to candy when made from crystals.

brewing.notes: Simmer dried apple for about ten minutes, with cinnamon if you wish, and sweeten after tasting. With instant granules, follow the package and start with less than you think.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, simply as a shelf product. The real division is between dried fruit and instant mix: read the ingredients for sugar and flavouring. Instant granules and powder are what shops and bazaars usually serve. Check whether a blend has black tea in it before assuming it is free of caffeine.
description:
Elma çayı is the apple tea offered to many a visitor in Turkey, a sweet, caffeine-free cup that sits apart from the strong black tea Turks drink every day.

There are two different drinks under one name. One is dried apple simmered in water, sometimes with spices. The other, and the one you are more likely to be handed in a shop, is an instant drink of concentrated apple juice and sugar.

The instant version is very sweet and uncomplicated. The fruit version is gentler, with some actual sourness, and needs simmering rather than a quick steep. Taste before adding any sugar.

If you liked the cup in the bazaar and want the same at home, instant packets will get you closest. If you want something better, try dried apples with a little cinnamon.
history: No solid record of its origin or inventor is known. It is often linked with shops and bazaars, where a cup is part of welcoming customers, and it is listed among the herbal teas most popular with foreign visitors to Turkey, along with rose hip and linden. In Turkish folk use it has been taken for digestive complaints and coughs.
